newsitem.title: USA: GPU'S new CEO enthusiastic about mergers.
newsitem.headline: GPU'S new CEO enthusiastic about mergers.

text.p: GPU Inc's new chief executive, Fred D. Hafer, views mergers and acquisitions enthusiastically as a means to the growth essential to the company's future success, GPU said Monday.
But one area of the new electric utility industry GPU does not plan on entering is bulk trading of electric power.
Hafer says it is not within GPU's recognized "skill sets," nor is it consistent with the company's accepted risk profile.
The 56-year-old West Reading, Pa., native takes over at GPU after the retirement May 31 of James R. Leva, 65, who served as chairman, president and CEO since 1992.
Hafer is the sixth chairman and CEO of GPU, an electric utility holding company formed in 1946.

He began his tenure as chairman, president and chief executive officer of GPU Monday by declaring that growth of GPU's core business -- delivering electricity -- will be one of the keys to GPU's success in a less regulated, more competitive electric utility industry.
"We're already as good as anyone out there -- and better than most -- at providing basic electric service. We intend to get even better," Hafer said.

"If there's a service we don't currently provide but should, we'll find a way to deliver it. We want our customers to know that we're always there for them, even as the electric power industry continues to undergo dramatic changes."
Hafer said that good companies capitalize on their strengths and recognize -- and take decisive action on -- their weaknesses.

"One of the keys to our success has been our swift reaction to the many changes in the industry," Hafer said. "We must now become more aggressive and outspoken in identifying threats and opportunities.

"We will, for example, take aggressive actions to grow our electricity distribution business, the backbone of our portfolio of businesses, both here at home and overseas. We will also look for opportunities to add related distribution businesses, such as natural gas and water distribution.
"With our primary strategic focus on the delivery of electricity and related services, we have been actively reviewing our portfolio of assets, particularly generation facilities," Hafer said.
Last year, for example, GPU closed two small fossil fuel-fired generating units in New Jersey.

And, in April, The company said it would explore the options of retiring the 620-megawatt Oyster Creek Nuclear Generating Station in Ocean County, N.J., early or selling it. A decision on Oyster Creek is expected by early autumn.
In response to inquiries that followed GPU's announcement about Oyster Creek, GPU said that it would entertain the possibility of selling the Three Mile Island plant, as well.
"It is my belief that to be a successful player in merchant generation in the future, a company will have to be both a low-cost provider and a big player, and GPU is not a big player," Hafer said.
GPU owns and operate some 9,000 megawatts of generation in Pennsylvania and New Jersey.

"It is likely that GPU will be faced with doing one of two things in merchant generation: Get bigger or get out. We're currently exploring those two options and we'll be in a position to make that decision later in the year," Hafer said.
He said GPU will continue to invest in contract generation domestically and abroad through the GPU International Group.
"We have said for some time that we are always exploring domestic and international growth opportunities, and we will continue to do so," Hafer said.
((-- New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610.))
